newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wanted to avoid wrong signal at wheat tender.
newsitem.headline: EU wanted to avoid wrong signal at wheat tender.

text.p: The European Union, which cut the amount of wheat released for export to 91,200 tonnes at a tender on Thursday, acted in response to the structure of bids and to avoid sending an overheated signal to the market, an EU official close to the European Commission said on Thursday.
It also cut its flour export refund to show that the five million tonnes (grain equivalent) already committed for export this season is reasonable for the time being, the official said.
But the move to lower wheat quantities -- from recent weekly volumes around 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes -- does not mean the EU is winding up its wheat exports just yet, the official said. teh
"We have taken such an advance (in volumes on last year)," the official said.

"It doesn't mean we will stop selling but we wanted to take it a little bit easy. When you look at the structure of the bids, if we had awarded too much it would have sent a wrong signal to the market," he added.
He noted that the volume of wheat sought for export at the tender, held each Thursday, had fallen sharply this week yet the refunds being sought were also much lower.
"It was so aggressive this week," the official said.
Authorities in France, where nearly all the wheat was taken this week, said bids for refunds were as low as 4.74 Ecus per tonne, implying a world price of around $170 per tonne.
The European Commission actually awarded 91,500 tonnes at a maximum refund of 7.49 Ecus per tonne for a price nearer $167.
Some traders had expected up to twice the volume with a maximum refund up to 9.45 Ecus.
The official said the award resulted from the circumstances of the bids and showed the EU was ready to "sit back for a few days" rather than gallop to the end of the season.
On flour, the EU decided to make its third cut in as many weeks in the value of a key subsidy to emphasise it was comfortable with export commitments just for now, he said.
"We have done five million tonnes. We wanted to make it clear we consider this a reasonable amount, for the time being," the official said.
EU officials say this week's move was not preceded by the kind of bidding for flour licences which forced the Commission to step in by rejecting the bids and cutting refunds in March.
At a previous level of eight Ecus per tonne, the refunds were already unattractive and had effectively halted exports, traders said.

Thursday's move brought the refund for the best class of flour down further to five Ecus per tonne. It also kept the refund below the rebate for wheat grain exports whereas in normal conditions it would be higher.
EU records show the trade area has released close to nine million tonnes of wheat for export since the season began on July 1 last year. Flour export commitments are just over five million tonnes.
Most traders have built their forecasts on an EU wheat grain export figure of some 10 million tonnes and flour exports of five million tonnes in the full year to June 30, 1997.
Flour millers have expressed anger about the recent cuts in refunds, saying they cannot operate without more EU support.
-- Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
